decisions.quote:
The results presented partly corroborate
those from the previous studies in which
Roter’s Interaction Analysis System was
used, but they also shed some new light on
the controversies found in the literature
about the relative relevance of instrumental
versus affective behavior.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly state that their findings only partly corroborate the earlier RIAS studies, confirming the role of task-related medical information in technical-medical proficiency while failing to corroborate the overall conclusion that task-related behavior is more important than affective behavior.

decisions.quote:
In Roter’s study, as well as in ours, the
quality of technical-medical care (‘‘profi-
ciency”) was better explained by RIAS task-
clusters than by RIAS socio-emotional clus-
ters. Also, in Roter’s study, as well as in ours,
“giving information” and, especially, “giv-
ing medical information” proved to be im-
portant in the assessed quality of care.
decisions.location: Discussion, p. 293 (also Abstract, p. 283; Introduction, p. 284; Methods, pp. 285-287; References 7-8, p. 296)
decisions.reason: Addressing the unresolved objection using the replicating text and both supplied primary abstracts (3695653.txt and 3695654.txt): Hall, Roter, and Katz (1987, "Task versus socio-emotional behaviors in physicians", Med Care 1987;25:399-412; Reference 7, represented in shipped row input_row_index 649, DOI 10.1097/00005650-198705000-00004) and Roter, Hall, and Katz (1987, "Relations between physicians’ behaviors and analogue patients’ satisfaction, recall and impressions", Med Care 1987;25:437; Reference 8, candidate target_index 1) are two companion articles from the same analogue-patient study of 43 primary care physicians interacting with two standardized simulated-patient cases, scored with RIAS, speech error counts, and filtered-audio vocal affect ratings. As the primary abstracts establish, Reference 7 (3695653.txt, shipped row 649) scored the encounter transcripts for "physician proficiency" and analyzed the internal associations among physicians' task-oriented, verbal socioemotional, and vocal-affect behaviors and their relation to physician proficiency (technical-medical quality). Reference 8 (3695654.txt) instead added ratings from 258 role-playing analogue patients to test associations between physicians' behaviors and analogue patients' satisfaction, recall of information, and global impressions. In Bensing and Dronkers (1992), "only general practitioner (GP) behavior is studied. GP’s behavior is related to panel-assessed quality of care on three separate dimensions (technical-medical, psychosocial, and the management of the physician-patient relationship)" (Abstract, p. 283). Bensing and Dronkers collect no patient satisfaction, patient recall, or patient impression data and do not retest the analogue-patient satisfaction/recall/impression findings unique to Reference 8. Instead, they treat References 7 and 8 jointly as a single study ("Roter’s study", "Hall and Roter’s study", "a study into the relative contribution of affective and instrumental behavior to the quality of care ('medical proficiency').7,8", p. 284), empirically retest the internal correlations among RIAS task, verbal socioemotional, and nonverbal affect measures (Tables 2-3) and their associations with panel-assessed quality of care/"proficiency" (Tables 4-5; Discussion, p. 293), and quote Reference 8 for the concluding call at the end of the two-paper sequence to replicate the study in a natural setting using video (p. 293). Because the underlying study and the specific empirical findings actually retested by Bensing and Dronkers are already represented by shipped row input_row_index 649 (Reference 7), Reference 8 is not a genuinely missing original target.
